yen0: The Medicine of the Future: Latest Scientific Advances | İhsan Eren
yen1: Latest scientific advances: short, sourced news on blood tests that detect Alzheimer's, new drugs ferried into the brain and gene-editing treatments.
yen2: Short, clear summaries of important advances at the cutting edge of medicine. Every story lists its source underneath.
yen6: Since May 2025, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved four tests that measure amyloid and tau changes in the brain from a blood sample. The latest two arrived in August 2026. These tests may make diagnosis easier, without the need for brain imaging or a lumbar puncture to collect spinal fluid.
yen7: Important: the tests are approved only for use in people with memory complaints, as part of an assessment by a doctor. They are not suitable for screening healthy people who have no symptoms.
yen10: A drug “shuttled” into the brain: trontinemab
yen11: Trontinemab, developed by Roche, is designed to cross the blood–brain barrier more easily with the help of a carrier. According to early-phase data presented at the AAIC Alzheimer's conference in July 2026, amyloid build-up in the brain fell below the threshold level at 28 weeks in 92% of patients who received the high dose.
yen12: The drug is not yet approved; large phase III trials are ongoing. Side effects such as microbleeds in the brain were seen in a small number of patients.
yen13: Source: Clinical Trials Arena, 16 July 2026
yen15: A gene therapy designed for a single baby
yen16: In the US, a baby named KJ had a rare genetic disease (CPS1 deficiency) that causes ammonia to build up in the body. In about six months, researchers developed and delivered a personalised gene-editing treatment that corrected the baby's own mutation.
yen17: It is one of the first examples to show that making a treatment “tailored to each patient” is possible for very rare diseases.
yen20: Casgevy, the first approved CRISPR treatment, is used for sickle cell anaemia and beta thalassaemia. In studies, 16 out of 17 patients with sickle cell disease had no pain crises, and 25 out of 27 patients with thalassaemia did not need blood transfusions. Gene editing carried out directly inside the body is also showing promising results.
yen21: Thalassaemia and sickle cell anaemia are common in Turkey, especially in the Mediterranean region. The treatment is expensive and is not available at every centre.
